title: Whiter than snow: the luminous mind
hookLine: white shows every scuff. so is a stained mind stained for good?
carry: the mind is luminous; its stains are visitors
tomorrow: what does a patch of sun on a wall have to do with any of this?
last: RED: THE COLOR, THEN THE FINE PEG.

lines: ONE SCUFF, AND IT'S NEVER NEW.
THE COLOR THAT SHOWS EVERY MARK.
cards: White sneakers show everything. One scuff on the first day and they never feel new again. A mind can seem like that too: one cruel thing said, one thing done that can't be undone, and it feels stained for good.
That was yesterday's question: can a stained mind ever come clean? Today's disc is white: white flowers, white cloth, something of silver, the color that shows every mark.
And a very old teaching answers more hopefully than the sneakers do.

teach.b: Here's the Buddhist answer, from a pair of very short suttas. The mind, the Buddha says, is luminous: bright, shining.
It gets stained by defilements that come in from outside, like visitors: greed, anger, confusion. And it can be freed of them. The stain is real.
It just isn't the mind's own color. A white cloth works that way too: dirt lands on it; it isn't made of dirt. Now a neighbor reaches for the same color.
A psalm in the Bibles of both Jews and Christians says, in the King James words, "Purge me with hyssop, and I shall be clean: wash me, and I shall be whiter than snow."
Two traditions, one image: a heart or a mind that can come clean, and a stain that doesn't have to stay. And one honest difference.
In the psalm, the one praying asks God to do the washing; cleanness comes as mercy, received. In the suttas, no one is asked.

teach.h: WASHED BY GOD, OR CLEARED BY PRACTICE.
teach.b: The brightness is said to be there already, and the clearing is the work of practice, done by the one who practices.
Each tradition says how in its own way, and neither needs the other to be wrong. What they share is worth saying out loud: a stain is not the whole story of a person.

how: In Theravada meditation the white kasina uses white flowers, cloth or a white or silver surface, noted as 'white, white'; the teaching that the mind is luminous and stained by visiting defilements is found in the Anguttara Nikaya.

o: a color of the dead, used to reflect on loss
the light said to shine from an awakened teacher
a disc of white, the color that shows every mark

games.q: two traditions, one color — tap the pairs.
p: the mind's own nature, in the sutta
washed by God, or cleared by practice

s: the Buddha taught that the mind is stained by nature
he called it luminous, stained by defilements that come in, and able to be freed of them.
a psalm in both the Jewish and Christian Bibles asks to be washed whiter than snow
Psalm 51. the shared hope: a heart can come clean.
the psalm and the sutta say exactly the same thing
the psalm asks God to wash; the sutta says the brightness is already there and practice clears the stains.

games.q: a friend says she'll never be a good person after what she said to her sister last year. what does the luminous-mind teaching offer her?
o: honesty: some stains really do go all the way through a person.
the stain is real, but it's a visitor, not her own color; it can be cleared.
it was a long time ago, so it doesn't matter and she can forget it.
games.why: the sutta doesn't pretend the stain isn't there. it says the mind is luminous and the stain came in, so it can be cleared.

practice: Take a plain white sheet of paper and rest your eyes on the white for a few breaths. Then, if you like, write one small word on it, a mark you'd like to set down. Look at how much white still surrounds it, and fold the page away.

wordCard.voice: White: odata in Pali. The color that shows every mark, and still isn't made of them.

orig.note: Pali: white, clean. The color disc held in mind with the plain word, white, white.

carryVoice: Your line: the mind is luminous, and its stains are visitors. The stain is real, and it isn't the cloth's own color. Until tomorrow.

sources.ref: Anguttara Nikaya 1.49-52 (Pabhassara Sutta: 'luminous is this mind', defiled by incoming defilements and freed from them)

sources.q: Purge me with hyssop, and I shall be clean: wash me, and I shall be whiter than snow.

sources.ref: Visuddhimagga 5 (the white kasina: white flowers, white cloth, or tin, lead or silver; noted as 'white, white')
